newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany confirms considering oil reserve sale.
newsitem.headline: Germany confirms considering oil reserve sale.

text.p: Germany is considering selling 7.3 million tonnes of oil from its strategic reserves in stages to help relieve strained government finances, a spokeswoman for the Economics Ministry said on Thursday.

She said Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt told selected reporters earlier this week the plan was one of several and that Bonn would decide whether to go ahead with it by July 11 when the cabinet is due to decide on a supplementary budget.

The sale of 7.3 million tonnes of crude oil from the reserve over the remainder of this year and 1998 would add some 100,000 barrels a day (bpd) to world supplies, the equivalent of a large new North Sea oilfield.

"Selling oil reserves is just one of several proposals to help solve Bonn's budgetary problems," the spokeswoman told Reuters. "It's not clear yet whether the plan will go ahead. The minister said this will be decided by July 11."
Rexrodt was quoted by the Handelsblatt business daily saying the oil stocks were worth some 1.4 billion marks.
Offering petroleum for sale could raise around 500 million marks a year in both 1997 and 1998, but Rexrodt said the sale would not have an impact on the world oil market.
Bonn is searching for ways to cut its budget deficit this year and next to meet the strict borrowing requirements for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
The German government also wants to step up the pace of privatisation, even though the Maastricht treaty does not allow the proceeds to be taken into account when calculating budget deficits.

Western countries built up strategic oil reserves following the 1970s Arab oil embargo to try and shield themselves from any oil price shocks. But, with oil prices moderate since the 1990-1991 Gulf crisis, that threat appears to have receded.
